transcript.text: Bosch SMS25AW00G, came back to E:09 on the display and the dishes are washed but stone cold. Is this an expensive fix?

It depends on which part is to blame, so it could be cheap or one of the dearer dishwasher repairs. I can't look up what E:09 means on your model just now, so I won't guess at it. But clean dishes that come out stone cold point to a heating problem whatever the code says. 1. The heater itself. The heating is done by a flow-through heater built into the circulation pump assembly, so a heater fault usually means replacing that whole assembly. That's typically the expensive outcome.
2. The temperature sensor. If it misreads, the machine may never switch the heat on, or may stop heating. This is a much cheaper part.
3. The wiring to the heater, including the loom running through the door hinge. A good heater that never gets power looks exactly like a dead one. One simple cause is also worth ruling out. A clogged filter can reduce water flow through a flow-through heater enough for it to cut out. 1. Clean the filter. Switch off and unplug first. Take out the lower rack, twist and lift out the filter in the base of the tub, and rinse it under the tap. If it was badly clogged, that may be the whole story.
2. Reset the machine. Leave it switched off at the wall for about five minutes. 3. Do a test run on an intensive or 65°C programme with a normal load. At the end, open the door carefully, as it may steam. Hot, steamy dishes mean the heater is working and the earlier fault may have been flow-related. Still cold, especially if the cycle ran much longer than usual or E:09 came back, suggests a genuine heating fault. If it's still cold after that, the next step is finding out which part has failed. Testing the heater and sensor means getting into the base of the machine, which is engineer territory for most people. Checking the pump/heater assembly is usually a fair-sized bill. A sensor or wiring fault would be well worth fixing. Let me know how the test run goes: hot or cold, and whether the code returns.
[Helpful to see: image "Where the filter is" — The filter sits in the base of the dishwasher, usually under the bottom spray arm. Twist it out anticlockwise and rinse it under a tap. Typical layout — your dishwasher may differ.]

I've already done the filter and it's clean. Power reset only clears the code briefly, it comes back next cycle. Both hot and eco programmes are cold. I do have a multimeter if testing the heater is safe to try?

On the multimeter: yes, it's safe electrically, as long as the machine is unplugged at the wall (not just switched off) and you only take resistance readings. Never test anything live. The real catch is access. On most Bosch dishwashers the heater connections are underneath. Getting to them usually means pulling the machine out, laying it on its back and taking off the base panel. That's a fair job, so it's only worth doing if you're comfortable with it. E:09 on Bosch typically means a fault in the flow-through heater or its heating circuit. That fits your cold washes on both programmes, the clean filter and the code coming back after a reset. The likely culprits, in order:
1. The flow-through heater itself (built into the circulation pump assembly). This is the most likely, and the dearer repair.
2. The wiring feeding it, including the loom through the door hinge. A good heater that gets no power looks exactly the same as a dead one.
3. The temperature sensor. It's less likely with this code, but it's a cheap part. If you want to test it:
1. Make it safe. Unplug it, turn off the water tap, and put towels down, because some water will come out when you tip it. Pull it out gently, watching the hoses.
2. Lay it on its back, remove the base panel, and find the heater's two power terminals on the pump/heater unit. Photograph the connectors before you pull them off.
3. Set the meter to ohms and measure across the two heater terminals. A healthy 2kW-ish heater typically reads somewhere around 20 to 35 ohms. - Open circuit or infinite means the heater has failed. That points firmly at the pump/heater assembly. - A normal reading means the heater is probably fine, so look next at the wiring and the door loom.
4. Also measure from each terminal to the metal body or earth. It should read open circuit. Any reading there means the heater is leaking to earth and has failed, even if step 3 looked fine. If the heater reads good, the next suspects are the wiring and loom, then the sensor. Tracing those is more involved, and that's where an engineer earns their money. On cost: a sensor or wiring fault is well worth fixing. If it's the heater/pump assembly, it's usually a sizeable bill, especially with labour. Ok, I'll give the heater test a go. Unplugged at the wall, panel off, I measured across the two heater terminals on the pump and it reads open circuit. What does that mean for the repair, and roughly what would it cost?

[Heading: Likely cause: heater]
An open circuit across the heater terminals means the heater has burnt out. Electricity can't flow through it, so it can't heat. That fits everything else: E:09, cold washes on every programme, a clean filter and the code coming back after a reset. I'm fairly sure about this. It also rules out the wiring and the sensor as the main problem, because a wiring fault would still leave the heater itself reading normally. One quick sanity check before you spend money. Make sure the connectors were pulled off and the meter probes were on the heater's own two terminals. Touch the probes together first to confirm the meter reads close to zero. If it still reads open circuit, the heater is dead. What it means for the repair: on Bosch dishwashers like this, the heater is normally built into the circulation pump. The heater usually can't be replaced on its own, so the fix is a new pump/heater assembly. On cost, I can't give you a reliable price or confirm the exact part for your machine. I also couldn't find a confirmed parts match for the SMS25AW00G. 1. Look for the rating label on the edge of the door. Note the full model number and the FD number, then check with Bosch spares or a reputable parts supplier. That's the only way to be sure you get the right assembly, as versions vary.
2. If you fit it yourself, you only pay for the part. It's manageable if you're handy and careful.
3. If an engineer fits it, the part plus labour is usually one of the dearer dishwasher repairs. On a budget machine it can come to a fair chunk of the price of a new one. Get a quote from Bosch's own service and a local independent so you can compare. Is it worth it? If the machine is fairly young and otherwise sound, a DIY replacement is usually good value. If it's older, has other niggles, or you'd be paying full engineer rates, compare the quote against a new dishwasher before deciding.
